predict.question: If you bring a magnet near a steel spoon, an iron nail, and a coin, what will happen?

options.text: Magnet pulls the iron nail strongly but may not pull the coin at all
Magnet pulls all three metal objects equally, since it attracts every metal
Magnet pulls nothing unless it touches the exact middle of the object

predict.why: Magnets attract only magnetic metals like iron and steel, not all metals such as most coins.

experiment.title: Testing the Magnet
steps: Predict which items the magnet will pull and which it won't.
Bring the magnet near the iron nail, steel spoon, coin, and paper clip one by one.
Note which objects get pulled and which don't.
Tie a string to a second magnet (or use a fridge magnet) and bring its ends near the first magnet's ends.
Flip one magnet around and bring the ends close again.
Notice if the magnets pull together or push apart each time.
experiment.note: Keep magnets away from mobile phones, cards, and pacemakers; do not let a child swallow small magnets.

say: Which object surprised you the most?
What happened when you turned the magnet around?
Can you guess why the coin didn't move?
avoid: Don't say 'magnets attract all metals' or explain poles before they try flipping it themselves.

notice.question: What did you see happen with each object and with the two magnets?
notice.lookFor: Child notices iron/steel objects get pulled but the coin doesn't, and that the two magnets sometimes pull together and sometimes push apart depending on which ends face each other.

hints.text: Look closely at which metal objects actually move toward the magnet.
Compare the nail's behaviour with the coin's behaviour.
Now compare how the two magnet ends behave when you flip one around.

reveal.explanation: Magnets attract only certain metals like iron, steel, nickel and cobalt — not all metals, so a coin made of copper or brass won't be pulled. Every magnet has two poles, a north and a south end. When two like poles (N-N or S-S) face each other, they push apart; when unlike poles (N-S) face each other, they pull together.
reveal.termMeaning: The two ends of a magnet where its pulling force is strongest, and which decide attraction or repulsion between magnets.

teachBack.prompt: Explain to a younger sibling why a magnet picks up a nail but not a coin, and why two magnets sometimes push each other away.

revisits.question: Will a magnet pick up an aluminium foil ball?
